findings.title: Server-Side JavaScript Injection via eval() of contribution fields
findings.attack_path: Authenticated user submits POST /contributions with preTax/afterTax/roth set to a JavaScript payload. handleContributionsUpdate calls eval(req.body.preTax) directly, executing attacker code in the Node.js process with full application privileges, enabling RCE and lateral movement to MongoDB and the host.
findings.remediation: Replace eval() with parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) (the commented-out fix already present in contributions.js) and reject non-numeric input before use.

findings.title: Passwords stored and compared in cleartext
findings.attack_path: UserDAO.addUser writes req.body.password verbatim into the users document and validateLogin compares fromDB === fromUser. Any read access to MongoDB (via NoSQL injection TM-007, a backup, or a compromised host) yields every account's plaintext password, including the admin account, enabling immediate full takeover and credential reuse against other systems.
findings.remediation: Hash passwords with bcrypt.hashSync on signup and verify with bcrypt.compareSync (the commented bcrypt-nodejs fix in user-dao.js).

findings.title: Sensitive PII (SSN, DOB, bank account, routing) stored unencrypted
findings.attack_path: ProfileDAO.updateUser persists ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting as cleartext fields in the users collection (the crypto encrypt/decrypt helpers are commented out). Any data-store read primitive (TM-007, host compromise, backup theft) exposes regulated financial PII for all users.
findings.remediation: Encrypt ssn/dob/bankAcc/bankRouting at rest using the crypto helpers stubbed in profile-dao.js with a per-record IV and a key from a secrets manager.

findings.title: NoSQL injection via unsanitized $where in allocations threshold
findings.attack_path: GET /allocations/:userId?threshold= passes threshold straight into a Mongo $where clause: `this.userId == N && this.stocks > '<threshold>'`. The $where operator runs server-side JavaScript in the database, so payloads like `0';while(true){}'` or `1'; return 1=='1` cause DB-side code execution, data exfiltration across all users, or denial of service.
findings.remediation: Drop $where entirely; use a typed comparison query. If a threshold filter is required, parseInt and range-check it (0-99) as the commented fix shows, and never interpolate user input into query JavaScript.

findings.title: Committed TLS private key in repository
findings.attack_path: artifacts/cert/server.key and server.crt are committed to source control. Anyone with repository read access obtains the private key, allowing TLS impersonation/man-in-the-middle of any deployment that reuses this key pair and decryption of captured traffic.
findings.remediation: Remove the key from git history, rotate the certificate, and provision TLS material at deploy time via a secrets manager rather than the repo.

findings.title: Hardcoded application secrets and ZAP API key in config
findings.attack_path: config/env/all.js hardcodes cookieSecret and cryptoKey, and config/env/development.js hardcodes a ZAP API key. With a known cookieSecret an attacker forges/ tampers signed session cookies; a known cryptoKey defeats any at-rest encryption that uses it.
findings.remediation: Load cookieSecret, cryptoKey and tooling keys from environment variables / a secrets manager with high-entropy values; never commit secrets.

findings.title: Default seed accounts with weak, predictable credentials
findings.attack_path: artifacts/db-reset.js seeds admin/Admin_123 and user1/user2 with documented passwords and isAdmin:true. If the seed runs against a real environment (docker-compose and app.json postdeploy invoke it), an attacker logs in as admin directly.
findings.remediation: Never seed default credentials in non-test environments; force a password change on first admin login and gate db-reset to test/dev only.

findings.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference on allocations by URL userId
findings.attack_path: displayAllocations reads userId from req.params instead of req.session, with no ownership check. Any authenticated user iterates /allocations/1, /allocations/2 ... to read every other user's portfolio allocations.
findings.remediation: Derive userId from req.session.userId (the commented fix), or enforce that the requested userId equals the session user / requires admin.

findings.title: Missing function-level access control on benefits administration
findings.attack_path: GET/POST /benefits are guarded only by isLoggedIn, not isAdmin (the isAdmin guard is commented out in index.js). Any authenticated non-admin user lists all non-admin users and rewrites arbitrary benefitStartDate values via POST /benefits.
findings.remediation: Add the isAdmin middleware to both /benefits routes as shown in the commented fix in routes/index.js.

findings.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via /research url parameter
findings.attack_path: displayResearch builds url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol and needle.get()s it, returning the body to the client. An attacker sets url to http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud metadata), internal services, or file/gopher targets to read internal resources and pivot inside the network.
findings.remediation: Remove the user-controlled url; pin the upstream host to an allowlisted finance API base URL and validate symbol against an alphanumeric pattern.

findings.title: Open redirect via /learn url parameter
findings.attack_path: GET /learn does res.redirect(req.query.url) with no validation. An attacker crafts /learn?url=https://evil.example to bounce authenticated users to a phishing site under the trusted application's domain.
findings.remediation: Redirect only to a fixed internal path or validate the target against an allowlist of relative paths / approved hosts.

findings.title: Stored XSS in memos rendered through outdated marked with autoescape disabled
findings.attack_path: POST /memos stores req.body.memo unsanitized; memos.html renders {{ marked(doc.memo) }} with swig autoescape disabled and marked 0.3.5 (known sanitize bypasses). A stored payload executes in every viewer's session, enabling session theft and admin compromise.
findings.remediation: Enable swig autoescape, upgrade marked and run output through a maintained HTML sanitizer (e.g. DOMPurify) before rendering.

findings.title: Reflected/stored XSS in profile due to wrong-context encoding and disabled autoescape
findings.attack_path: Profile fields (website, firstName, etc.) are stored unfiltered and rendered with autoescape off; the website value is HTML-encoded but then placed in a URL/link context, so a javascript: or attribute-breaking payload executes when the profile is viewed.
findings.remediation: Enable autoescape globally and use context-correct encoding (encodeForURL for link contexts) plus a URL scheme allowlist for website.

findings.title: No transport encryption — application served over plaintext HTTP
findings.attack_path: server.js starts http.createServer (the https block is commented out). Credentials, session cookies and PII traverse the network in cleartext, so a network-positioned attacker captures admin credentials and session tokens.
findings.remediation: Terminate TLS (enable the commented https.createServer or front with a TLS-terminating proxy) and enable HSTS via helmet.

findings.title: Session cookies lack HttpOnly/Secure flags and use a guessable name
findings.attack_path: The express-session config omits cookie.httpOnly and cookie.secure (both commented out). Combined with the XSS findings (TM-012/TM-013), document.cookie reads the session id; over plaintext HTTP (TM-014) it is also sniffable, enabling session hijacking.
findings.remediation: Set cookie { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge }, rename the cookie, and serve over HTTPS.

findings.title: Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing routes
findings.attack_path: csurf is imported but app.use(csrf()) is commented out and no token is emitted in forms. An attacker auto-submits a cross-origin form to POST /profile, /contributions or /benefits, mutating victim data (or admin benefits) using the victim's ambient session.
findings.remediation: Enable csurf, inject the token into every form, and set SameSite cookies as defense in depth.

findings.title: Username enumeration via distinct login error messages
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest returns 'Invalid username' vs 'Invalid password' on failed logins (the unified-message fix is commented out), letting an attacker enumerate valid accounts to focus credential-stuffing.
findings.remediation: Return a single generic 'Invalid username and/or password' message for all login failures.

findings.title: Weak password policy and no anti-automation on auth
findings.attack_path: validateSignup accepts any 1-20 char password (strong-policy regex commented out) and there is no rate limiting or lockout on POST /login, so trivial brute force / credential stuffing succeeds against weak passwords.
findings.remediation: Enforce the strong PASS_RE policy and add rate limiting/lockout (e.g. express-rate-limit) plus MFA on login.

findings.title: ReDoS via catastrophic backtracking in bank routing regex
findings.attack_path: handleProfileUpdate validates bankRouting with /([0-9]+)+\#/, a nested-quantifier pattern. A crafted input of many digits without a trailing # forces exponential backtracking, pinning the single-threaded Node event loop and denying service to all users.
findings.remediation: Use a linear regex such as /([0-9]+)\#/ (the commented fix) or anchored /^[0-9]+#$/.

findings.title: Session fixation — session id not regenerated on login
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest sets req.session.userId without calling req.session.regenerate() (signup does, login does not). An attacker who fixes a victim's session id pre-auth retains an authenticated session after the victim logs in.
findings.remediation: Call req.session.regenerate() on successful login before assigning userId.

findings.title: Verbose error handler leaks stack traces to clients
findings.attack_path: errorHandler renders the raw error object into error-template. Unhandled errors (including DB and injection failures) return internal paths, query fragments and stack details to the attacker, aiding exploitation of TM-001/TM-004.
findings.remediation: Return a generic 500 page to clients and log details server-side only; differentiate dev vs prod verbosity.

findings.title: Outdated and vulnerable dependencies plus disabled security middleware
findings.attack_path: package.json pins old releases (mongodb 2.1.x, swig 1.4.x, marked 0.3.5, needle 2.2.4) and disables helmet, dont-sniff-mimetype and CSP in server.js. Known CVEs in these components plus absent security headers (no X-Frame-Options, no CSP, x-powered-by exposed) broaden clickjacking, MIME-sniffing and supply-chain exposure.
findings.remediation: Upgrade dependencies, run npm audit/Snyk in CI, and enable helmet (frameguard, CSP, noSniff, hsts) and app.disable('x-powered-by').

findings.title: Container build runs as packaged but production hardening left commented; default MemoryStore session store
findings.attack_path: The Dockerfile leaves the production chown/chmod read-only hardening commented out, and express-session uses the in-memory MemoryStore (leaks memory, single-instance, lost on restart). Combined, a compromised app process can tamper with the writable image, and session state is a memory-exhaustion DoS vector.
findings.remediation: Enable the commented read-only filesystem hardening, run as non-root (already USER node), and use a production session store (Redis/Mongo) with bounded memory.

findings.title: Log injection / forging via unsanitized username in console logs
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest logs the raw attempted userName (the ESAPI/CRLF-strip fix is commented out). An attacker embeds CRLF and forged log lines into userName to corrupt logs, hide activity, or mislead responders.
findings.remediation: Strip/encode CRLF in any user input before logging (userName.replace(/(\r\n|\r|\n)/g,'_')) or use a structured logger.

findings.title: Mass-assignment / type-confusion exposure on profile and contributions inputs
findings.attack_path: Profile and contributions handlers consume req.body fields without type checks; a comment in profile.js warns that string methods on HPP-supplied arrays cause DoS, and unvalidated $set in ProfileDAO permits writing unexpected fields. Crafted array/object params can break logic or trigger errors.
findings.remediation: Validate/whitelist each field's type, coerce to string/number explicitly, and reject array/object values where scalars are expected.
